background.head: The problem
background.text: Honduras has 15,492 public schools in this dataset. 1,130 of them already have a working internet connection. The other 14,362 do not, and connecting them is not a procurement exercise — for most of the country the physical infrastructure that would carry the connection does not exist yet. The question this model answers is narrow and practical: given a fixed amount of money and five years, which schools should the country connect, in which order, and what should it build to do it?

background.head: How a school gets connected
background.text: The plan uses fixed wireless rather than fibre. A school counts as connected only when two things are true at the same time. First, there has to be a radio mast within 10 km of it carrying a WISP unit — the transmitter that actually broadcasts the internet signal. Second, the school itself needs a device package: the computers and receiving equipment that let it use the signal. Neither half is any use alone. A school surrounded by coverage but without equipment is not connected, and nor is a fully equipped school with no transmitter in range.

background.head: Why some schools cost nine times more than others
background.text: A WISP unit has to sit on a mast, and Honduras already has 7,297 cell towers. Where one of those happens to stand within 10 km of a school, the country only has to fit it with a WISP unit at $5,500 and buy the school its devices at $7,300 — roughly $12,800 to connect that school. Where no tower is in range, one has to be built first, at $100,000. The same school then costs about $112,800. That nine-fold difference is what drives almost everything else in this analysis: it is why coverage grows unevenly, and why some departments stall.

background.head: The money, and the catch
background.text: The budget is $125M over five years, released as $25M a year and split between the 18 departments in proportion to how many unconnected schools each one has, with anything unspent carried into the next year. The catch is that connecting a school is not a one-off purchase. Every connected school costs $3,820 a year to keep running — electricity, bandwidth, maintenance. Connect a school in year 1 and it draws that charge in each of years 2 to 5, which is $15,280 that can no longer be spent on building anything. Connecting schools early is therefore more expensive than connecting the same schools late, out of the same pot.

background.head: What the model is
background.text: A mixed-integer linear programme, or MILP. The decisions are yes-or-no — build this tower in year 3 or not, fit this mast with a WISP unit or not, buy this school its devices or not — which is the "integer" part, and the costs and the budget add up in straight lines, which is the "linear" part. A solver then searches the space of every legal five-year plan and returns the one that connects the most schools by year 5. The result is not a good guess or a simulation: within the stated assumptions it is provably the best plan available, which is what makes it a useful yardstick to measure real policy against.

background.head: Why there are two plans
background.text: Left to itself the solver discovers that waiting is efficient. It spends almost nothing for four years, avoids four years of running costs, and then connects nearly everyone at once in year 5. That is the Unrestricted plan, and it is the upper bound on what $125M can buy. No government can show nothing for four years, so the second plan adds annual targets: by each year t, a set share of the originally unconnected schools must be online — 10%, 15%, 20%, 25% and 30% — and the solver is penalised for falling short. That is the Milestone-constrained plan. The difference between the two is the price of visible progress, and it is what the rest of this brief measures.

glossary.def: Wireless internet service provider equipment fitted to a mast. It broadcasts the signal, and covers schools within 10 km. $5,500.
A mast that a WISP unit can sit on. Either already standing (7,297 of them) or newly built at $100,000.
The computers and receiving equipment a school needs to use the signal. $7,300 per school, one-off.
Capital expenditure — the one-off cost of building towers, fitting WISP units and buying devices.
Operations and maintenance — the recurring $3,820 a year that every connected school costs to keep running.
An annual coverage target the plan is penalised for missing. Set at 10%, 15%, 20%, 25% and 30% of the originally unconnected schools.
Honduras's 18 first-level administrative regions. Budget is allocated to each one separately, which is why coverage varies so much between them.
Holds a device package AND sits within 10 km of a WISP-equipped mast. Both conditions, in the same year.

bluf: On a $125M five-year budget, an unrestricted plan connects 12,409 of 12,578 unconnected Honduran public schools — 98.7%. Imposing annual milestones of 10–30% of remaining unconnected schools cuts that to 9,363, or 74.4%.

The 3,046-school gap is not a budget shortfall. It is recurring cost: every school connected early draws $3,820 a year in O&M for the rest of the horizon, and that spending displaces the capital that would have connected others in year 5.
Each percentage point of early visible progress costs about 125 schools connected by 2030.

Exposure is uneven. Four departments fall below 37% under milestones, against a 74.4% national figure, because they depend on new towers at $100,000 each and receive budget in proportion to their unconnected school count rather than to the cost of reaching them.

judgements.text: Milestones cost 3,046 schools, or 24.3 percentage points of year-5 coverage, on an identical budget. The constraint binds on timing, not on money.

The mechanism is O&M crowding out CAPEX. The unrestricted plan concentrates 99.4% of connections in year 5 and spends $278,860 on O&M across the horizon; the milestone plan spends $23,309,640, which is 28% of its own capital programme.

Milestones also strand equipment. 1,183 purchased device packages — $8,635,900 — sit at schools that never receive coverage within the horizon, against 40 packages ($292,000) in the unrestricted plan.

New-tower dependence drives departmental variance. Six departments reach 100% unrestricted; under milestones, Islas de la Bahía falls to 24.4%, Olancho to 29.8%, Yoro to 31.6% and Francisco Morazán to 36.4%.

The plan creates a permanent liability that outlasts it. Sustaining the unrestricted end-state costs $47.4M a year from 2030; the milestone end-state costs $35.8M. Neither figure is inside the $125M capital budget.

Coverage is not the only binding constraint on the unreached. Of the 169 schools the unrestricted plan never connects, 58 lie within 10 km of a WISP-equipped site and 34 of those already hold a device package. The report's claim that all 169 lie outside coverage does not hold.

brief.milestone_cost: Milestones bind on operating cost, not capital. A school connected in year 1 draws $3,820 in O&M in each of years 2 to 5 — $15,280 that is then unavailable for capital. The milestone plan front-loads 2,943 connections into years 1 to 4 and pays $23,309,640 in O&M across the horizon; the unrestricted plan defers almost everything to year 5 and pays $278,860. The difference, roughly $23M, is close to the $33.96M of capital the milestone plan never deploys, and it buys 3,046 fewer schools. Dividing the loss by the 24.22-point coverage gap gives about 125 schools per percentage point of early visible progress.
brief.department_exposure: Departments are allocated budget in proportion to their unconnected school count, not to the cost of connecting them. Where existing towers are dense, a school costs about $12,800; where a new tower is needed first, about $112,800 — a factor of nine. Under the unrestricted plan this is absorbed, because the solver defers spending and buys towers wherever they are cheapest per school reached. Under milestones each department must show annual progress from its own proportional share, so the departments that need towers spend their allocation on a handful of expensive sites and then stall. Islas de la Bahía (24.4%), Olancho (29.8%), Yoro (31.6%) and Francisco Morazán (36.4%) are the clearest cases; Olancho alone accounts for 96 of the 169 schools the unrestricted plan cannot reach at all.

recommendations.head: Calibrate milestones against the O&M–CAPEX trade-off
recommendations.text: Treat the 125-schools-per-percentage-point figure as the price of visible progress and set λ from it explicitly. A milestone schedule that starts lower and steepens in years 4 and 5 buys most of the political signal at a fraction of the coverage cost.

recommendations.head: Allocate budget by cost-to-connect, or set a regional coverage floor
recommendations.text: Proportional-to-need allocation systematically underfunds new-tower departments. Either weight allocations by the cost of reaching each department's unconnected schools, or impose a minimum coverage percentage per department and let the solver find the cheapest way to meet it.

recommendations.head: Budget the post-2030 run-rate before committing
recommendations.text: Full coverage implies $47.4M a year in O&M from 2030, which is 38% of the entire five-year capital budget, every year, indefinitely. A connectivity programme without a standing O&M line will decay back toward its starting point.

recommendations.head: Treat the excluded schools as a separate problem
recommendations.text: The 1,784 schools with no candidate tower within 10 km, and most of the 169 the model cannot reach, are not short of WISP budget — they are outside WISP geometry. They need fibre or satellite, and costing them against this programme's per-school figures will understate the requirement.

limitations: Deterministic only. Demand, costs and build times are treated as known. The stochastic extension is out of scope here.

A school counts as connected when it holds a device package and lies within 10 km of a WISP-equipped tower. Line of sight, terrain, spectrum, backhaul capacity and subscriber capacity per site are not modelled.
Costs are point estimates with no inflation, no procurement variance and no discounting.

The milestone plan's capital and O&M sum to $107.8M against a $125M budget, leaving about $17M unspent. This is a consequence of allocating budget per department with carry-over: some departments cannot spend their share. It is not slack available nationally.
The 1,784 excluded schools and the 1,130 already connected cannot be reproduced from the files in this repository, so those figures are carried from the report rather than recomputed.

The link drawn between a selected school and a site is derived — the nearest WISP-equipped site active by the selected year — not the solver's own assignment, which was never exported. It agrees with the model's connected flag for 12,408 of 12,409 unrestricted connections.
School coordinates are rounded to five decimals (about 1 m) in the site payload.
Device deployment at schools that already had working devices is not re-costed.

method.connection: A school is connected in year t when it holds a device package and lies within 10 km of a tower carrying a WISP unit by year t.
method.chain: Investment follows a strict prerequisite chain: a tower must exist before a WISP unit can be installed on it, and a WISP unit must cover a school before that school's device package produces connectivity. Existing towers skip the first step.
method.allocation: The $125M budget is split as $25M per year and allocated across the 18 departments in proportion to their unconnected school counts, with unspent funds carried over.

1 if school s holds a device package by year t
1 if site j carries a WISP unit in year t

the sites within 10 km of school s
the penalty per school of milestone shortfall, set to 10

equations.label: Objective
equations.says: Connect as many schools as possible by year 5. The second term is the milestone penalty: in any year where fewer schools are online than the target demanded, the shortfall is charged at π = 10 per school. Drop that second term and you have the Unrestricted plan; keep it and you have the Milestone-constrained one. Everything else about the two models is identical.

equations.label: A school needs its own equipment
equations.says: A school cannot be counted as connected in a year unless it holds a device package that year. Coverage alone is not connectivity.

equations.label: A school needs a transmitter in range
equations.says: A school also needs at least one WISP-equipped site within 10 km. If every mast in range is bare, the right-hand side is zero and the school stays unconnected however much equipment it has.

equations.label: A transmitter needs something to stand on
equations.says: A WISP unit can only exist at a site that either already had a tower, or has had one built there in this year or an earlier one. This is the prerequisite chain: tower, then WISP unit, then a connected school.

equations.label: Spending is capped, department by department
equations.says: Everything built and everything run, summed over department e's sites and schools from year 1 to year T, has to fit inside that department's cumulative allocation. The last term is the one that does the damage: $3,820 is charged for every year a school stays connected, so an early connection keeps drawing down the budget that later construction would have used.

equations.label: Every decision is yes or no
equations.says: You cannot build two thirds of a tower. This integrality is what makes the problem a mixed-integer programme rather than ordinary linear algebra, and it is why solving it is hard.

method.notation_note: Shown as the binding structure rather than the full constraint set. Omitted for brevity: that a connected school stays connected in later years, and that equipment once bought is not re-bought.

mismatches.head: MilestonesSites.csv repeats site_ids, so the report's milestone infrastructure totals are row counts
mismatches.text: The file holds 6,261 rows for 5,307 distinct site_id values. 921 ids repeat, and 68 of those carry contradictory rows — the same site appears once with got_wisp=0 and once with got_wisp=1. Counting rows gives the report's 164 new towers and 313 WISP units; counting distinct sites gives 156 and 302, and CAPEX falls from $84,536,900 to $83,676,400. NoMilestoneSites.csv has no duplicates, so the unrestricted figures are unaffected.
mismatches.resolution: Map geometry deduplicates by site_id with union semantics, so no site is drawn twice. Headline KPIs keep the report's row-count figures so the site and the report agree; the distinct-site figures are shown here.

mismatches.head: The old README's 250-schools-per-percentage-point figure was wrong
mismatches.text: 3,046 schools divided by a 24.22-point gap is 125.8, not 250. The figure appeared to have been derived against a 12.2-point gap.
mismatches.resolution: Corrected to about 125 throughout the site and in the README.

mismatches.head: Not all 169 unreached schools lie outside coverage
mismatches.text: The report states that the 169 schools the unrestricted plan never connects lie outside any candidate tower's 10 km WISP radius. Measured against the model's own output, 111 have no site within 10 km, 24 have a WISP-equipped site in range but no device package, and 34 have both a WISP-equipped site in range and a device package — at a median 5.64 km, so these are not boundary artefacts. Those 34 satisfy both halves of the stated connection rule yet are flagged unconnected, which suggests a per-site capacity limit or a precomputed school-site adjacency narrower than a plain 10 km radius.
mismatches.resolution: The claim is not repeated. The school-to-site link is labelled as derived, never as the solver's assignment.

mismatches.head: The 1,784 excluded schools cannot be recomputed from this repository
mismatches.text: The only candidate set published here is the 7,297 existing towers, and those leave 54% of the optimisation set beyond 10 km — so the model must also have had candidate new-tower locations, which were never exported. The baseline school list cannot substitute: it contains 1,935 duplicate rows, its 1,130 connected schools collapse to 920 distinct records, and joining it to the output CSVs leaves 148 rows unmatched rather than 1,784.
mismatches.resolution: The 15,492 / 1,130 / 1,784 / 12,578 setup figures are carried from the report with source notes. No baseline school layer is drawn, because it could not be drawn honestly. The 7,297 existing towers ship as a clearly labelled context layer.
